## H1 finding: yes, model family matters — but the honest magnitude is small

**Setup.** Dropped `fnlwgt` (a census sampling weight, not a subject attribute) and `education` (verified exactly 1-to-1 with `education-num`). Missing categoricals kept as an explicit `Missing` level. Stratified 80/20 split; hyperparameters chosen per family by 5-fold CV ROC-AUC on train only; each family refit and scored once on the untouched test set. Uncertainty from a 2000-replicate bootstrap **paired** across models (same resamples for every model), so differences are compared like-for-like.

| Family | CV AUC | Test AUC | Test acc |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hist Gradient Boosting | 0.9282 | **0.9283** | 0.872 |
| Random Forest | 0.9192 | 0.9194 | 0.867 |
| MLP (64,32) | 0.9120 | 0.9128 | 0.860 |
| Logistic Regression (C=0.5) | 0.9064 | 0.9054 | 0.854 |
| Decision Tree (depth 10) | 0.9070 | 0.9035 | 0.860 |
| GaussianNB | 0.8728 | 0.8756 | 0.764 |
| k-NN (k=50) | 0.8685 | 0.8608 | 0.841 |
| Majority baseline | 0.500 | 0.500 | 0.761 |

**Key numbers.** Full spread across serious families = **0.0675 AUC** (primary metric). Boosting − LogReg = **+0.0229** [0.0197, 0.0260], p ≈ 0. RF − LogReg = +0.0140 [0.0115, 0.0166]. Top-3 spread is only 0.0155. CV and test agree to ~0.001 everywhere, so these aren't split artifacts.

**Interpretation.** Every difference is statistically significant — with ~9.8k test rows, the bootstrap resolves gaps far below what matters practically. The substantive story is the *shape* of the ranking: the gradient is steep only where a family's inductive bias is wrong for this data (k-NN suffering in ~100-dim one-hot space; GaussianNB's independence/normality assumptions collapsing on the spiky `capital-gain`), and nearly flat among the five reasonable choices, which span just 0.025 AUC. Adult has a strong, largely additive signal (marital status, education, capital-gain, hours), so a linear model captures most of it; boosting's edge comes from the remaining interactions and the sharp `capital-gain` thresholds.

**Caveats another researcher might handle differently:** single split rather than repeated/nested CV; modest grids and no XGBoost/LightGBM (unavailable here), so boosting's edge is if anything a floor; no class-weighting (ROC-AUC is rank-based); duplicates retained. Judging on accuracy instead of AUC would compress everything, since the 76% majority baseline is already high.

Files written: `analysis.py`, `result.json`, plus `model_comparison.json` with the full per-model metrics, chosen hyperparameters, and bootstrap CIs.

parsed_result.summary: Yes, but the effect is bounded and concentrated at the tails: across eight model families held-out test ROC-AUC spans 0.067 (0.928 for HistGradientBoosting down to 0.861 for k-NN). Boosted trees beat a tuned logistic regression by 0.023 AUC (paired-bootstrap 95% CI [0.020, 0.026]), a small but unambiguous margin, whereas mis-specified families (k-NN 0.861, GaussianNB 0.876) lose two to three times as much. Family choice therefore matters mainly for avoiding poor fits; among reasonable choices (LogReg, tree, MLP, RF, boosting) the whole range is only ~0.025 AUC.
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: Held-out test ROC-AUC spread across model families (best Hist Gradient Boosting - worst k-NN, excluding majority baseline)
parsed_result.direction: Hist Gradient Boosting > Random Forest > Logistic Regression > ... > k-NN; boosted trees best, differences among strong families small (top-3 spread 0.015 AUC)
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Target: >50K = positive (23.9% prevalence). Dropped fnlwgt (census sampling weight) and education (redundant with education-num). Missing categorical values ('?' -> NaN) kept as an explicit 'Missing' level rather than imputed. Numerics median-imputed + standardized; categoricals one-hot encoded with levels below 1% frequency grouped as infrequent. Single stratified 80/20 train/test split (seed 0); hyperparameters chosen by 5-fold stratified CV ROC-AUC on train only via small per-family grids, then refit on full train and scored once on the held-out test set. Primary metric ROC-AUC (threshold- free, appropriate for the 3:1 imbalance); PR-AUC/accuracy/F1 at 0.5 reported secondarily. No class-weighting or resampling was applied -- probabilities were left as-is since ROC-AUC is rank-based. Uncertainty from a 2000-replicate bootstrap of the test set, paired across models (identical resamples), giving CIs and two-sided p-values for family-vs-family differences. Families compared: majority baseline, GaussianNB, L2 logistic regression, k-NN, CART, random forest, HistGradientBoosting, MLP(64,32). Another researcher might have used repeated/nested CV instead of a single split, wider hyperparameter grids or external boosters (XGBoost/LightGBM), target/ordinal encoding for trees, dropped duplicate rows, or judged on accuracy/F1 at a tuned threshold -- accuracy in particular compresses the gaps because the 76% majority baseline is already high.
